antipatterns: app/Models/Coupon.php:35,41,48 - writes redeemed_count back onto the route-bound $this from inside the transaction closure. It is a hidden side effect, and the controller (RedeemCouponController.php:21) relies on it to get the count right.
app/Models/Coupon.php:28 - returns ?CouponRedemption with null meaning 'used up'. That makes the controller branch on a null sentinel instead of letting a domain exception carry the 409.
app/Http/Controllers/RedeemCouponController.php:15-16 - builds the 409 response by hand in the controller, so the error message is in the controller while the business rule is in the model.
Neither the row lock nor DB::transaction has a retry or attempts setting. Lock-wait timeouts under heavy contention would come back as 500s (all three implementations share this).
strengths: Locks the coupon row with lockForUpdate inside DB::transaction, then checks for an existing redemption, checks the cap, inserts and increments. The unique (coupon_id, user_id) index backs this up, so it holds across servers on MySQL.
Dispatches the event after the transaction commits, and only when wasRecentlyCreated is true, so retries and double-submits cannot fire it twice.
Uses route model binding {coupon:code} for the 404, an invokable controller, the #[Fillable] attribute, and whereBelongsTo.
Keeps the counter out of mass assignment: redeemed_count is not fillable.

Thorough tests: a pre-exhausted coupon has no side effects, an existing redeemer still gets 200 after the coupon is used up, 6 users against a cap of 3, and a test that the unique index rejects duplicates. The factory has an exhausted() state and the exception class is imported properly.

antipatterns: app/Models/Coupon.php:40 - the model throws Symfony's ConflictHttpException, which puts an HTTP concern in the domain model. A domain exception with a render() method would be cleaner.
tests/Feature/RedeemCouponTest.php:114 - uses an inline fully-qualified class name instead of importing UniqueConstraintViolationException.
tests/Feature/RedeemCouponTest.php:122 - the test name says 'competing redemption inserted mid request', but the test only covers a redemption that already exists. It does not simulate a race.
No retry or attempts setting on the transaction. Lock-wait timeouts under contention would come back as 500s.
strengths: Locks the coupon row (whereKey()->lockForUpdate()) inside the transaction, then uses firstOrNew, checks the cap, saves and increments. Combined with the unique index, both the once-per-user rule and the hard cap hold across servers.
Fires the event outside the transaction, only when wasRecentlyCreated is true. The controller uses the same flag to choose 201 or 200.

The thinnest controller of the three: route model binding {coupon:code} and one call to the domain method. The model's redeemFor() reads well and uses setRelation so the count comes back without an extra query.
Uses #[Fillable], throw_if and whereBelongsTo, and keeps redeemed_count out of fillable.
Tests cover the guest 401 both with and without an Accept header, use assertExactJson for the repeat response, check an existing redeemer after the coupon is used up, and check the unique index.

antipatterns: app/Http/Controllers/Api/CouponRedemptionController.php:21-53 - all the transaction, locking, business rules and event dispatch are in the controller action.
app/Http/Controllers/Api/CouponRedemptionController.php:31,41,44 - returns a positional tuple [$redemption, $coupon, $created] from the closure instead of using wasRecentlyCreated or a value object.
app/Http/Controllers/Api/CouponRedemptionController.php:15,22-26 - looks up the coupon by hand and calls abort(404) instead of using route model binding {coupon:code}.
app/Models/Coupon.php:15 - redeemed_count is mass-assignable, so a stray fill() could reset the counter.
Uses the old-style protected $fillable property even though the #[Fillable] attribute is available in Laravel 13.40. The event uses an empty {} constructor body over multiple lines.
tests/Feature/CouponRedemptionTest.php:104 - builds an array imperatively with a foreach loop, and line 113 uses an inline fully-qualified class name.
No retry or attempts setting on the transaction.
strengths: The concurrency approach is correct: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the coupon row inside a transaction, then check for an existing redemption, check the cap, insert and increment, backed by the unique index.
Dispatches the event after commit and only for the request that created the redemption.
Because the lock covers the coupon lookup itself, there is no window between binding and locking.
Tests cover 401, 404, 201 with a single event, a repeat returning 200 with no new event, 409 with a message, and the cap of 3 against 6 users.

v.rationale: All three use the same concurrency approach, and it is the right one: lockForUpdate on the coupon row inside DB::transaction, check for an existing redemption before the cap, increment, back it with a unique (coupon_id, user_id) index, and dispatch the event after commit only for the request that created the redemption. All test suites pass (impl-2: 11, impl-3: 10, impl-1: 11). My probes passed in all three and were then deleted: cap of 0 returns 409 with a message, 409 and 404 return JSON without an Accept header, a repeat reports the current redeemed_count after other users redeem, the event carries a persisted model, and a lowercase code returns 404. I found no real bugs, so the ranking comes down to idioms. impl-2 ranks first: route model binding, the thinnest invokable controller, and a clean redeemFor() using firstOrNew, throw_if and setRelation. Its cost is an HTTP exception thrown from the model, plus a small mess (empty Requests directory, a misleading test name). impl-1 is nearly as good and has slightly richer tests and factory states. It loses ground for returning null to mean 'used up', building the 409 in the controller, and writing redeemed_count back onto the bound $this from inside the closure. impl-3 is correct but puts all the logic in the controller, returns a tuple from the closure, skips route model binding, makes the counter mass-assignable, and uses the old-style $fillable.
